questions.text: How does call differ from apply?
options: call takes arguments one by one, apply takes an array. Both set this
apply sets this, call does not
call invokes the function, apply only binds this
No difference: both ignore the first argument

questions.text: Can call replace this on a function that was already bound?
options: Yes, the latest call always wins
Yes, if you pass the same object
No: bind already fixed this, and call does not change it
No, because bind returns nothing

questions.text: Why do forEach and map take a second argument, thisArg?
options: It becomes this for an ordinary callback during the loop
It also replaces this for an arrow
It is the initial accumulator, as in reduce
It is the number of iterations

questions.text: What does new do with a function that was already bound?
options: new uses the bound object and does not create a new one
new ignores the bound this and creates a new object. Bound arguments stay
Such a function cannot be called with new
new drops both this and the bound arguments

questions.text: A second bind replaces the this fixed by the first bind.
call and apply can replace this on an arrow.
An ordinary class method pulled off an instance loses this.
A class arrow field remembers the instance even if the field is called on its own.
How does the const self = this trick work for a nested function?
questions.answer: self stores the method’s this in a variable. The inner function reads self from the closure, because its own this is no longer the object.

questions.text: Why does an arrow callback in forEach see the method’s this, while a plain function does not?
questions.answer: An arrow has no this of its own and takes the method’s. A plain function gets this from forEach: without thisArg that is undefined in strict mode.

questions.text: Where does a class method live, where does an arrow field live, and how does that affect this?
questions.answer: One method lives on the prototype, and this comes from the call. An arrow field is created on each instance and closes over that instance’s this.

questions.text: What remains of bind if the function is later called with new?
questions.answer: The bound this is dropped: new creates its own object. Arguments bound with bind are still prepended.

questions.text: What happens to this with const { show } = box?
options: show stays tied to box
The link to box is lost: it is now an ordinary function with no object before the call
this becomes undefined forever, even for box.show()
Destructuring calls show immediately

questions.text: Why does one method on the prototype print a different n for two instances?
options: The engine copies the method into each instance with its own n
There is one method, but this in a.read() is a and this in b.read() is b
The prototype stores a separate this for every new
The second instance overwrites the first instance n

questions.text: What is this inside a method called through super.show()?
options: A separate base-class object
The prototype that owns show
The same derived instance on which the method was called
undefined: super resets this

questions.text: How does a function that reads a constructor argument differ from one that reads this.n?
options: The argument is closed over, so call with another object does not replace it. this.n depends on the call
Both read the same thing: the constructor this forever
A constructor argument is this
The closure sees the this of the call that invokes the function

questions.text: const { show } = box keeps this equal to box.
A prototype method called as a.read() gets this equal to a.
super.show() sets this to a base instance separate from the derived one.
A function that closed over a constructor argument changes its answer when called via call with another object.
Why does destructuring a method lose the object?
questions.answer: const { show } = box copies the function reference. show() is then called with no object on the left, so this is no longer box.

questions.text: How does one prototype method serve different instances?
questions.answer: A single function lives on the prototype. instance.method() sets this to that instance, so it reads that instance's own n.

questions.text: Which object becomes this in super.method()?
questions.answer: The same instance on which the derived method was called. super only picks the base function; this is not replaced with a separate base object.

questions.text: When a function created in a constructor reads a parameter rather than this, what does call change?
questions.answer: Nothing about that value. The parameter lives in the closure. call replaces only this, and only if the function reads this.n.
